title: Wait, Did I Write This?
author: Managing the Future
summary: This article reviews a Harvard Business Review study on private-equity-backed CEOs — a high-stakes laboratory for CEO effectiveness because these leaders must produce outsized results fast, with more than half failing to meet expectations before the investment period ends. The study identified 53 'superperformers' who achieved an average 6.2x multiple on invested capital (more than double the typical target) and found five disciplines that set them apart. The author frames these disciplines against his own CEO teaching framework, noting that all five align closely with what he has been training leaders on for over a decade. The five disciplines are: (1) strategic clarity — translating investment thesis into a 3-5 year plan and treating clarity as a drumbeat, not a quarterly conversation; (2) talent — rigorously and quickly assessing whether current leaders can scale, and raising the bar rather than just filling gaps; (3) relentless focus — limiting active initiatives to three to five 'big rocks' and actively resisting the organizational tendency to accumulate priorities; (4) agile operating rhythms — designing deliberate meeting cadences and review structures rather than inheriting the previous regime's habits; and (5) accountability culture — understanding that culture is what leaders tolerate, not what they profess, and building structures that connect values to actual behavior. The author argues that this research represents a step toward the long-overdue professionalization of the CEO role, which has lacked an agreed-upon framework compared to every other functional role in an organization.
points: The PE-backed CEO context is an unusually useful laboratory because the hard constraint (make the business much more profitable, fast) strips away the comfort margin that allows ordinary CEO failure modes to persist undetected — more than half of PE-backed CEOs fail before the investment period ends.

Strategic clarity must be treated as a drumbeat, not a quarterly conversation — superperforming CEOs continuously reinforced a single-page three-year plan throughout the organization rather than restating strategy at annual planning cycles and assuming the field would hold it.

The talent discipline is primarily about the cost of waiting: every CEO knows intellectually they need A-players in critical seats, and the practical failure mode is giving someone a third chance at a standard they've missed twice — the authors call this 'organizational drag' and identify it as a major performance killer.

Focus requires active counter-pressure against a natural organizational tendency to accumulate initiatives: superperformers limited active priorities to three to five and used visual tools (dashboards, stop/start/continue lists) to reinforce what was and was not in scope — not as novelty but as discipline.

Culture is what leaders tolerate: superperforming CEOs built accountability not through slogans or perks but through specifying what each role owns, how it collaborates, and where decision authority sits — translating stated values into actual behavioral expectations in writing.
quotes: It can feel like one of the labors of Hercules. If the regular CEO role is a tightrope walk, the PE-backed version has a faster-fraying rope and a bigger canyon to cross. That makes it a particularly good laboratory for studying CEO behaviors and outcomes.

They excel at translating an investment thesis into a three-to-five-year strategic plan. They clearly define and communicate their organization's most important objectives, priorities, and value creation drivers, and then ensure alignment and focus across the organization.
[Super-performing CEOs] understand strategic clarity is not a quarterly conversation, it's a drumbeat.

[High-performing CEOs] rigorously assess current leaders and make difficult talent decisions quickly to avoid organizational drag. And they don't just fill gaps; they raise the bar by bringing in proven scale leaders who 'know what good looks like' and can hit the ground running.
Every company I have looked at that has not been doing well has been because of a failure to focus.

[High-performing CEOs] limited active initiatives to three to five major priorities and made sure those were crystal clear throughout the organization. They created visual tools like dashboards and stop/start/continue lists to reinforce focus and communicate tradeoffs.

The high-performing CEOs in our study understand that culture is what they tolerate. They don't rely on perks or slogans to drive it, and they're intentional about the tone they set, the values and behaviors they reward, and the norms they allow to persist.
